**LOS ANGELES** — Maurice Jarre, the French-born composer whose lush, unforgettable scores for epic films such as "Lawrence of Arabia" and "Doctor Zhivago" earned him three Academy Awards and cemented his place among the giants of 20th-century film music, has died. He was 84.

Jarre died of cancer at his home in Los Angeles, surrounded by family, according to representatives for the composer. His death was confirmed earlier this week.

Over a career spanning more than five decades, Jarre wrote music for some 150 films, but he will forever be linked to his celebrated collaboration with British director David Lean.

## An Enduring Partnership

Jarre's work with Lean produced some of the most recognizable film music ever composed. His score for "Lawrence of Arabia" (1962), with its soaring, exotic themes evoking the endless sweep of the desert, won him his first Oscar and announced his arrival as a major cinematic voice.

Three years later, "Doctor Zhivago" (1965) brought him a second Academy Award and gave the world "Lara's Theme," a melody so popular it became a worldwide hit and remains instantly familiar to audiences today. A third Oscar followed for "A Passage to India" (1984), the final feature Lean would direct.

"David Lean gave me the freedom to create music on the largest possible canvas," Jarre once reflected on the partnership that defined his early career.

## Reinventing His Sound

Rather than resting on the orchestral grandeur that made him famous, Jarre embraced reinvention. In the 1980s, he became a pioneer of electronic scoring, trading full orchestras for synthesizers on films such as Peter Weir's "Witness" (1985) and "The Year of Living Dangerously" (1982).

The shift showcased a restless creative spirit unwilling to be confined by past success, and it introduced his work to a new generation of filmmakers and audiences. He continued to move fluidly between the electronic and the orchestral, adapting his sound to the demands of each story.

## Tributes Pour In

News of Jarre's death prompted an outpouring of tributes from across the film and music worlds, where colleagues remembered both his artistry and his generosity.

Fellow composers hailed him as a master craftsman whose melodies could define a film's emotional core in just a few notes. Collaborators recalled a warm, passionate man whose enthusiasm for music never dimmed.

His influence extended within his own family: his son, Jean-Michel Jarre, became one of the world's best-known electronic musicians, carrying forward a legacy of innovation.

## A Lasting Legacy

Born in Lyon, France, in 1924, Jarre initially trained in engineering before turning to music, studying at the Paris Conservatory. He began his career composing for the theater before moving into film, ultimately becoming one of the most sought-after composers in Hollywood.

Beyond his three Oscars, he received numerous Golden Globe and BAFTA honors, and his themes endure as fixtures of the cinematic canon.

Jarre is survived by his family, including his son Jean-Michel.

His music, colleagues noted, will outlast them all — a testament to a composer who understood that a single melody, well written, could echo across generations.

The Berlin recognition underscored the universal appreciation for an artist whose work had become woven into the fabric of world cinema.
